base_origin: Existing short self-contained Q&A prompts, checked alongside new original topic cards

base_cards.front: Who is King of Scotland when the play begins?
back: Duncan.

base_cards.front: Which new title does Macbeth receive soon after meeting the witches?
back: Thane of Cawdor.

base_cards.front: Whose descendants do the witches predict will become kings?
back: Banquo’s.

base_cards.front: Who escapes when Banquo is murdered?
back: Fleance.

base_cards.front: Who discovers Duncan’s body?
back: Macduff.

base_cards.front: Who becomes king at the end of the play?
back: Malcolm.

base_cards.front: Who describes his own motive as “vaulting ambition”?
back: Macbeth.

base_cards.front: Who says “Out, damned spot”?
back: Lady Macbeth.

base_cards.front: Which wood appears to move towards Dunsinane?
back: Birnam Wood.

base_cards.front: Whose ghost does Macbeth see at the banquet?
back: Banquo’s.

base_cards.front: Who kills Macbeth?
back: Macduff.

base_cards.front: What is the term for a speech in which a character speaks private thoughts aloud, usually while alone?
back: Soliloquy.

base_cards.front: What is the term for a situation in which the audience knows something a character does not?
back: Dramatic irony.

base_cards.front: Complete Lady Macbeth’s image: look like the “innocent flower”, but be the what beneath it?
back: Serpent.

base_cards.front: Does the audience see Duncan being murdered onstage?
back: No. The murder happens offstage.

base_cards.front: Who warns Macbeth about the “instruments of darkness”?
back: Banquo.

base_cards.front: Who says “Turn, hellhound, turn!”?
back: Macduff.

base_cards.front: Which apparition gives the promise about “none of woman born”?
back: The Second Apparition.

base_cards.front: What is regicide?
back: The murder of a king.

base_cards.front: What is usurpation?
back: Taking power without a legitimate right.

base_cards.front: What does hubris mean?
back: Excessive pride or overconfidence.

base_cards.front: What is hamartia?
back: A tragic error or flaw contributing to downfall.

base_cards.front: Which title does Duncan give Malcolm when naming his successor?
back: Prince of Cumberland.

base_cards.front: Give two duties Macbeth has towards Duncan before the murder.
back: As Duncan’s **subject**, Macbeth owes him loyalty.
As Duncan’s **host**, Macbeth should protect him.
He is also Duncan’s relative, giving him a further reason to protect him.

base_cards.front: What does “Stars, hide your fires” suggest about Macbeth’s desires?
back: He wants darkness to **conceal** his ambition.
Wanting to hide it suggests that he recognises it is **morally wrong**.

base_cards.front: Explain the image “vaulting ambition”.
back: Ambition is compared to **leaping too far**, like a rider overshooting.
It suggests that excessive ambition can cause a **fall**, anticipating Macbeth’s destruction.

base_cards.front: How does Lady Macbeth use Macbeth’s ideas about manhood to influence him?
back: “When you durst do it, then you were a man” makes murder a test of **masculinity**.
She pressures him to prove his courage instead of following his moral objections.

base_cards.front: How do Macbeth’s “ocean” and Lady Macbeth’s “little water” present different responses to Duncan’s murder?
back: Macbeth imagines an entire ocean cannot remove his **guilt**.
Lady Macbeth treats it as a small, practical problem of washing away the **evidence**.

base_cards.front: What does Macbeth mean by a “fruitless crown”?
back: He fears that his kingship will not produce a lasting **dynasty** for his family.
Banquo’s predicted descendants make the crown feel insecure and unfulfilling.

base_cards.front: Explain one effect of “full of scorpions is my mind”.
back: The **metaphor** fills Macbeth’s mind with painful, poisonous creatures.
It makes his anxiety seem like torment from which he cannot escape.

base_cards.front: How does the banquet scene expose the weakness of Macbeth’s authority?
back: His response to Banquo’s ghost makes him lose control in front of his guests.
The public display of fear undermines the appearance of a confident, secure king.

base_cards.front: How does “Be innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck” show a change in the Macbeths’ relationship?
back: Macbeth withholds the details of the murder plan from Lady Macbeth.
This contrasts with their earlier **partnership** and shows her growing exclusion.

base_cards.front: Why is the attack on Macduff’s family important to the presentation of Macbeth?
back: It shows his violence targeting **innocent, vulnerable people**.
The audience sees the human cost of his **tyranny**, beyond his own fears.

base_cards.front: What alternative view of masculinity does Macduff express in “I must also feel it as a man”?
back: Being a man includes feeling **grief and love**, not hiding them.
His response challenges the idea that courage requires emotional hardness.

base_cards.front: How is the prophecy about Birnam Wood fulfilled?
back: Malcolm’s soldiers carry branches to **conceal their numbers**.
Their advance makes the wood appear to move towards Dunsinane.

base_cards.front: Why does the promise about “none of woman born” fail to protect Macbeth from Macduff?
back: Macduff reveals that he was cut from his mother’s womb: “Untimely ripped”.
This fulfils the prophecy in a way Macbeth did not expect, exposing its **misleading reassurance**.

base_cards.front: How does Lady Macbeth’s hand-rubbing connect with her earlier response to guilt?
back: It echoes her earlier claim that “A little water” could clear the deed.
Her inability to remove the imagined stain shows that **guilt cannot simply be washed away**.

base_cards.front: What does “Life’s but a walking shadow” suggest about Macbeth near the end?
back: A shadow has little substance and does not last.
The **metaphor** expresses his feeling that life and his achievements have become empty.

base_cards.front: What does Banquo mean by keeping his “allegiance clear”?
back: He wants to keep his **loyalty untainted**.
He will not gain honour by sacrificing his **conscience**.

base_cards.front: Why does Banquo’s question about his own “oracles” complicate his character?
back: He hopes the witches’ promise for his descendants will be true.
He is **tempted**, although he does not commit murder to make it happen.

base_cards.front: How does calling Macbeth “wicked” change his opening reputation?
back: It contrasts with the Captain’s praise of “brave Macbeth”.
Even a witch now identifies the former defender as a source of **evil**.

base_cards.front: Explain the contrast between “innocent flower” and “serpent”.
back: The flower suggests a harmless **appearance**.
The serpent represents the concealed **danger and betrayal** underneath.

base_cards.front: What does Lady Macbeth’s reference to her father reveal?
back: Duncan’s resemblance to her father stops her from killing him herself.
It reveals an emotional limit to the **cruelty** she tries to perform.

base_cards.front: What does “king-becoming graces” suggest about good leadership?
back: A king needs **moral qualities**, such as justice and mercy.
Holding a royal title is not enough to make someone a **worthy ruler**.

base_cards.front: How does “blood will have blood” develop the violence theme?
back: The repeated word suggests that bloodshed produces further **bloodshed and consequences**.
Macbeth fears retaliation, but continues the violence that creates it.

base_cards.front: How do regicide and usurpation describe different parts of Macbeth’s rise?
back: **Regicide** names the killing of Duncan.
**Usurpation** names Macbeth’s seizure of the crown without a legitimate right.

base_cards.front: Explain the religious metaphor “The Lord’s anointed temple” in Act 2, Scene 3.
back: Macduff compares Duncan’s body to a **sacred building**.
Its violation presents the murder as an attack on sacred authority, as well as a political crime.

base_cards.front: Why is it useful to call the witches catalysts rather than the sole cause of Duncan’s murder?
back: Their predictions **encourage Macbeth’s ambition** and speed up events.
They do not command the murder: Macbeth understands the objections and **chooses** to act.

base_cards.front: What does Macbeth’s “full of scorpions” metaphor reveal after he becomes king?
back: The poisonous creatures make his thoughts seem **painful and dangerous**.
Gaining power has produced **insecurity**, which encourages further violence, rather than peace.

base_cards.front: How does Malcolm’s test of Macduff differ from Duncan’s earlier judgement?
back: Duncan trusts men who betray him, while Malcolm **tests loyalty** before accepting it.
Macduff’s distress at the prospect of another bad ruler shows that he puts **Scotland before personal allegiance**.

base_cards.front: When answering the 15-mark extract question, how should you use evidence?
back: Select words, actions or shifts from **across the printed passage**.
Explain their meanings and effects while keeping the answer focused on that passage.

base_cards.front: How can you connect violence to a question about Macbeth’s ambition?
back: Explain how the desire for the crown leads to **Duncan’s murder**.
Then show that fear of losing power drives further killing; keep the violence linked to the question’s focus.

additions.front: Why does Duncan naming Malcolm matter to Macbeth?
back: Malcolm becomes the named heir. Macbeth sees a new obstacle between his desire and the crown, so his response exposes ambition beneath outward loyalty.

additions.front: How does the Porter scene contribute beyond comic relief?
back: The imagined gate of hell connects the castle to moral corruption. The knocking also increases the threat that the hidden crime will be discovered.

additions.front: What is blank verse?
back: It is unrhymed verse, usually using iambic pentameter: five beats built around an unstressed–stressed pattern.

additions.front: Why is naming blank verse alone insufficient analysis?
back: You must explain how the actual rhythm, wording or line arrangement shapes meaning in that passage. Not every line follows a perfectly regular pattern.

additions.front: How does Macbeth change between his first and second visits to the witches?
back: At first he encounters them while returning from battle. Later he actively seeks their predictions, showing a growing dependence on supposed certainty.

additions.front: Analyse “false face must hide what the false heart doth know”.
back: The repeated “false” links outward performance with inward dishonesty. Macbeth deliberately chooses concealment, so the line preserves his responsibility for the crime.

additions.front: What does “To be thus is nothing, but to be safely thus” reveal?
back: The repeated “thus” refers to kingship, but “safely” makes security the new demand. Gaining the crown has intensified fear instead of ending ambition.

additions.front: How does excluding Lady Macbeth from the Banquo plot develop their relationship?
back: Macbeth begins directing violence without sharing his full plans. Their earlier cooperation gives way to secrecy and emotional separation.

additions.front: Why does Fleance escaping matter?
back: Macbeth cannot secure the future he wants. The escape leaves Banquo’s promised line a threat and prevents the murder from giving Macbeth lasting reassurance.

additions.front: Why should the dagger and Banquo’s ghost not be treated as identical stage events?
back: The dagger belongs to a private speech before the murder. The ghost interrupts a public banquet after Banquo’s death, exposing Macbeth’s disturbance to his guests.

additions.front: Why is Banquo a foil rather than simply Macbeth’s opposite?
back: Both are interested in the predictions, but Banquo voices caution and does not murder to fulfil them. Their shared temptation makes their different choices significant.

additions.front: How does “Bleed, bleed, poor country!” develop kingship?
back: Repetition and personification make Scotland seem like an injured body. The focus moves from Macbeth’s private security to suffering under his rule.

additions.front: How does Macduff challenge a violent definition of manhood?
back: He insists “I must also feel it as a man”. The line joins masculine identity with grief and compassion, rather than treating emotion as weakness.

additions.front: What can we safely conclude from the doctor’s response to Lady Macbeth?
back: He observes disturbed behaviour and recognises the limits of medicine. The scene links her suffering to conscience, but does not prove supernatural possession.

additions.front: How does the sleepwalking scene reverse Lady Macbeth’s earlier control?
back: Earlier she directs Macbeth and treats washing as a practical solution. Later her repeated actions and broken speech cannot remove the imagined stain.

additions.front: What distinction matters when discussing Malcolm’s ending?
back: He promises restoration and invites the nobles to his coronation. The play does not show the results of his reign.

additions.front: How should evidence differ between the extract and whole-play tasks?
back: The extract answer analyses the printed passage closely. The whole-play essay selects relevant moments from across the play to develop its argument.

additions.front: How does clothing imagery present insecure authority?
back: Images of borrowed or badly fitting clothing suggest that possessing a title does not make Macbeth fit for the role. Link the particular image to its speaker and moment.

additions.front: What is the difference between an aside and a soliloquy?
back: An aside is spoken so that other characters are conventionally not hearing it. A soliloquy presents an extended private train of thought; both give the audience privileged access.

additions.front: Why should the witches not remove Macbeth’s responsibility in an essay?
back: Their predictions influence his expectations, but they do not command Duncan’s murder. His debates, concealment and later independent plots show repeated choices.
